name: Gareth Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollins Systems, a family firm of about twenty people that makes stock-control software for timber yards and builders' merchants. I'm a junior developer, so I mostly fix reports, like why a yard's count of fence posts doesn't match what's on the shelf. I like that our customers are real businesses with forklifts and mud, not apps nobody needs. The hard part is that I'm still slow, and the codebase is huge.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you at work and at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Frank Hollins started the company with his brother thirty years ago, and he still walks round every desk on Monday mornings. My mentor is Alan, who's been there almost as long. Outside work, I'm engaged to Rhiannon, a dental nurse, and we're getting married next summer at the church where her parents married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd expect, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, like a lot of things from the big tech firms. At work I'd say good old-fashioned know-how wins again. I don't post online, but I'd say it in the pub with my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I've never used any of these AI tools and I didn't fancy starting. Frank Hollins looks after his people, so if nothing radical changes, my job's as safe as any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep learning from Alan the old way, by reading the code and asking questions. We'd keep saving for the wedding and put the rest into our joint savings, which is about four months. If someone made me try an AI tool I would, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Settled. My mind would be on the wedding, not on computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Frank Hollins looks after his people. Has he ever had to let anyone go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, in the bad year after the pandemic. Frank Hollins, who owns the firm, paid two laid-off people for three months out of his own pocket. I trust Frank more than I'd trust any big company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the wedding costing you, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 12,000 all in, split between us and some help from Rhiannon's parents. It's a big chunk, but it's the one time we'll do it. We'd still have savings left after.

say: AI was **oversold**, like a lot of things from big tech firms.
**Old-fashioned know-how** wins again, I'd say in the pub.
think: I'd be **relieved**, since I never fancied starting with AI tools.
Frank Hollins **looks after his people**, so my job feels safe.
do: Keep learning from **Alan** by reading code and asking questions.
Keep saving for the **wedding** and the joint savings pot.
Try an AI tool only **if made to**.
feel: **Calm** and settled, with his mind on the **wedding**.
S0.quote: Frank Hollins, who owns the firm, paid two laid-off people for three months out of his own pocket. I trust Frank more than I'd trust any big company.
fieldNote: His sense of safety rests on **loyalty** to a family-owned firm.
He doesn't use AI and **sees no reason** to start in this picture.
The **wedding** dominates his plans and his spending.

steps.text: Keep fixing stock reports and learning from Alan
Save for the 12,000 wedding and keep joint savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Coding's on that list. That's not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have every right to use whatever tools make them competitive, that's how it should work. I'd also say young people need proper apprenticeships, not just being told to learn AI on YouTube. At work I'd keep quiet and let Frank decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. Frank's a good man, but if a competitor cuts prices using AI, he'd have to keep up. The juniors who don't use the tools, which is me, would be the easiest to let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Alan to show me how he'd use one of these tools, so I'm not completely behind. I'd probably push the wedding to a smaller do, maybe 8,000, and keep the difference as savings. I'd also ask my uncle Ray, who fits kitchens, whether he'd take me on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. I'd be checking Frank's face on Monday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd shrink the wedding. How would Rhiannon feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd understand, but she'd be sad. Her mum has had the church booked in her head since Rhiannon was ten. We'd keep the church and cut the reception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your uncle's kitchen fitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's real work with your hands, and nobody's writing an app to fit a kitchen worktop. I did summers with Ray when I was at college. He's always said I've got the patience for it.

say: Businesses have **every right** to use tools that keep them competitive.
Young people need **proper apprenticeships**, not YouTube lessons on AI.
think: If a competitor cuts prices with AI, **Frank would have to** keep up.
Juniors who **don't use the tools**, like me, go first.
do: Ask **Alan** to show him one AI tool.
Shrink the wedding to about **8,000** and save the difference.
Ask uncle Ray about **weekend kitchen fitting**.
S1.quote: Nobody's writing an app to fit a kitchen worktop.
fieldNote: He defends firms' **freedom to automate** even as it threatens him.
He'd cut the **wedding reception** but keep the church.
His fallback is **family**: uncle Ray's kitchen-fitting work.

steps.text: Ask Alan to demonstrate one AI coding tool
Shrink the wedding budget from 12,000 to 8,000
Fit kitchens with uncle Ray at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 is the year after our wedding. That's no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not for the government to stop it, but families and churches will have to look after each other. I'd say people should go back to learning trades. At work I'd say we should all be honest with Frank about what we can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Hollins Systems either sells or shrinks to a few people, and I'm not one of them. My job is all at a keyboard, so 2028 is my date. The robots for hands-on work come in 2031, so Ray's kitchens would have three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd move the wedding to a small church service and a meal for the families, around 3,000. I'd start with Ray at weekends right away and ask about going full time within the year. I'd keep every bit of savings in the bank, and we'd look at living with Rhiannon's parents if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It'd sit on my chest at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years with Ray, then robots arrive. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I don't like not knowing. Maybe people would still want a person they know in their house. I'd trust that the Lord and my family would see us through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at church about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask people to pray for the families affected, and I'd ask the older men if they need help with jobs around the house. That's how our church works. Somebody always knows somebody.

say: It's not for the government to stop it; **families and churches** must help each other.
think: Hollins Systems **sells or shrinks**, and I'm not one who stays.
Ray's **kitchen fitting** gets three more years before the robots.
do: Cut the wedding to a **3,000** church service and family meal.
Start with **Ray at weekends** and aim for full time.
Keep savings in the bank and consider **living with** Rhiannon's parents.
feel: **Alarmed**, with worry sitting on his **chest** at night.
S2.quote: AGI by 2028 is the year after our wedding.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** to justify switching to kitchen fitting.
His faith and **church network** are his safety net, not the state.
Beyond 2031 he has **no plan** and admits it.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to a 3,000 church service
Join uncle Ray's kitchen fitting full time within the year
Live with Rhiannon's parents if money runs short
Keep all savings in the bank, no extras

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people to sort themselves out if they don't wait for someone else to do it. I'd say it's a good moment for firms to take on apprentices in trades. I wouldn't say much at work beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still think my developer job goes before 2031. But five years means we can have the wedding as planned, and I can learn Ray's trade properly. I'd rather be a good kitchen fitter than a bad developer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding as planned next summer. From year one I'd do Saturdays with Ray, and by year three I'd leave Hollins Systems and go full time with him. I'd keep four months saved and not spend on anything fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. It feels like a plan I'd be proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather be a good kitchen fitter than a bad developer. Have you thought that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly, a few times. I'm slow at coding, and I'm not getting fast enough. This would just give me a reason to say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Frank Hollins say when you left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd shake my hand and tell me I'm welcome back any time. He'd mean it, even if there's no job to come back to by then.

say: There's time if people **don't wait** for someone else to fix it.
Firms should take on **trade apprentices** now.
think: I'd rather be a **good kitchen fitter** than a bad developer.
do: Keep the **wedding** as planned next summer.
Do **Saturdays with Ray**, then go full time by year three.
Keep **four months** saved and avoid anything fancy.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, with a **plan** he'd be proud of.
S3.quote: I'd rather be a good kitchen fitter than a bad developer.
fieldNote: AI gives him **permission** to leave a job he wasn't thriving in.
Five years lets the **wedding** go ahead unchanged.
Loyalty to **Frank Hollins** stays strong even as he plans to leave.

steps.text: Keep the wedding at the church next summer
Work Saturdays with uncle Ray learning kitchen fitting
Leave Hollins Systems for Ray's business by year three
Keep four months of costs saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Well, that's a long time in anyone's book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the people who complain later will mostly be the ones who did nothing. I'd say young men like me should learn something with their hands alongside their job. At church I'd say the same to the younger lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could have kids before any of this lands. My job at Hollins Systems would be fine for a good few years. I'd still not use the AI tools, which might come back to bite me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and do Saturdays with Ray from year two. Rhiannon and I would try for our first child after the wedding, maybe in 2028. Around 2031 I'd decide whether to go full time with Ray, with savings of about six months by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Mostly fine, but it'd be there at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not using the tools might come back to bite you. Why not start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Habit, mostly, and I don't trust them. I'd rather understand what I'm doing than have a machine guess. I'd start if Frank told me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would kids come up in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years feels like a normal life. With two years, I'd be scared to bring a baby into the world. With ten, I'd have a trade by the time any child was at school.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and complainers will be those who did nothing.
Young men should learn something **with their hands** alongside their job.
think: Ten years means we could have **kids** before it lands.
Not using **AI tools** might come back to bite me.
do: Keep his job and do **Saturdays with Ray** from year two.
Try for a **first child** with Rhiannon around 2028.
Decide on **full time** with Ray around 2031 with six months saved.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly fine but with worry at the back of his **mind**.
S4.quote: With two years, I'd be scared to bring a baby into the world. With ten, I'd have a trade by the time any child was at school.
fieldNote: Long warning opens **starting a family**, which he'd avoid otherwise.
He'd only use AI if **Frank told him** to.
**Traditional** views show in advice to younger men at church.

steps.text: Keep his Hollins Systems job for a good few years
Do Saturdays with Ray from year two
Try for a first child with Rhiannon around 2028
Build savings to six months by 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right after the wedding, before we've had a chance to settle. What would help is proper paid apprenticeships for grown men, not just teenagers. Ray can't afford to pay me a full wage while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what faith has to do with it. People will need something steady when work goes, and for me that's church and family. A screen can write my code, but a screen can't sit with my nan on a Sunday.

headlineQuote: A screen can write my code, but a screen can't sit with my nan on a Sunday.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** junior developer at Hollins Systems, a family software firm.
He **never uses AI** and trusts the firm's owner, Frank Hollins, more than big companies.
His **traditional views** put family, church and trades ahead of government help.
His **wedding** with Rhiannon shapes his money plans in every picture.
He plans a move into **kitchen fitting** with uncle Ray, using the robot gap.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands right after the **wedding**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults, so Ray doesn't have to pay a full wage.
